title: A Second Oven
focus: Modals of probability and polite requests (would you mind, could you possibly, is bound to)

lines.text: Mr Castillo, thank you for coming in. I've looked at your application for a loan to buy a second oven.
Thank you. I hope the figures speak for themselves.
They're encouraging, though there are a couple of points I'd like to clarify. Would you mind explaining the dip in sales last winter?
Of course. A road near the shop was closed for repairs for two months, so customers simply stayed away. It shouldn't happen again.
Can you be sure of that?
As sure as anyone can be. The work was finished in spring, and the council has said that nothing similar is planned.
That's reassuring. Now, the second oven would let you bake more, but would there be enough customers to buy it all?
I believe so. We've turned away large orders from cafés because we couldn't produce enough. Two of them might well order regularly once we can supply them.
Could you possibly put that in writing, even informally?
I'll ask them. I'm fairly certain they'd be happy to write a short letter.
That would strengthen the case considerably. Is there any chance of repaying the loan faster if sales grow?
There ought to be. In a good year, we'd be able to repay early, as long as there's no penalty.
There's a small one, but it should be possible to negotiate it down. I'll need to take this to my manager, who is bound to ask about collateral.
I understand. I'd be prepared to offer the old oven as security, though it must be worth very little now.
It might not be necessary. I'll let you know our decision within the week.

questions.q: How does Mr Castillo feel about the winter dip in sales?
options: Confident that it was a one-off
questions.explain_es: Actitud. 'It shouldn't happen again... nothing similar is planned.'

questions.q: What does Ms Pryce imply by 'It might not be necessary'?
options: She does not need her manager's approval
The offered security may not be required
The old oven is worth a lot
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Responde a su oferta de dar el horno viejo como garantía.

questions.q: Why does Ms Pryce ask for a letter from the cafés?
options: To strengthen the evidence of demand
questions.explain_es: Propósito. 'That would strengthen the case considerably.'

questions.q: What does Mr Castillo say about repaying early?
options: He would prefer to pay a penalty
He would like a longer loan
He could do so if there is no penalty
He could never afford to do so
questions.explain_es: 'We'd be able to repay early, as long as there's no penalty.'

questions.q: Mr Castillo says that the road closure lasted a whole year.
questions.explain_es: Dice: 'closed for repairs for two months'.

questions.q: He says he has turned away large orders from cafés because of limited capacity.
questions.explain_es: 'We've turned away large orders from cafés because we couldn't produce enough.'

dictation: A road near the shop was closed for repairs for two months, so customers simply stayed away.
That would strengthen the case considerably.

title: What Is a Library For?
focus: Evaluative and hedging language (arguably, it could be argued, by no means)

lines.text: Tonight we're asking whether councils should keep funding public libraries when so much is available online. Mr Hollis?
Libraries are by no means worthless, but we have to be realistic. Borrowing has fallen steadily, and every pound spent on a quiet building is a pound not spent on, say, care for the elderly.
It could be argued that you're measuring the wrong thing. Loans are only part of what a library does. People come to use computers, to find work, to join a class, or simply to sit somewhere warm.
Those are real benefits. But arguably other services could do those things more cheaply.
Could they? A library is one of the few places where you don't have to buy anything to be welcome. That's rare, and it's hardly something that can be replaced by an app.
Mr Hollis, is that persuasive?
To a degree. I'd concede that the social role is underrated. My difficulty is that it's hard to put a figure on it, and councils must justify every decision.
Which is precisely the problem. What isn't measured tends to be cut. By no means does that mean it has no value.
Fair. So what would you suggest, measuring it differently?
Yes, and some libraries already do. They record the number of people helped with job applications, or children attending reading sessions. That's data a finance committee can use.
That I could work with. It's not an easy sell, though. Ministers like new buildings, not maintenance.
Could libraries share space with other services?
That's already happening. Some have a health clinic or a council advice desk on site. It's arguably the best of both worlds.
I'd support that, as long as the books aren't an afterthought.
Nor should they be. Reading is still the core.
A sensible place to stop. Thanks to you both.

questions.q: How does Mr Hollis view the social role of libraries?
options: He finds it irrelevant to councils
He concedes that it is underrated
He thinks that it is overrated
questions.explain_es: Actitud. 'I'd concede that the social role is underrated.'

questions.q: What does Ms Njeri imply by 'What isn't measured tends to be cut'?
options: Councils may undervalue what they cannot measure
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Señala que lo difícil de medir se recorta, aunque tenga valor.

questions.q: Why does Ms Njeri mention helping people with job applications?
options: To argue libraries should become job agencies
To show that books are obsolete
To give examples of measurable benefits
questions.explain_es: Propósito. 'That's data a finance committee can use.'

questions.q: What does Mr Hollis say about the financial case?
options: Libraries are too expensive to run
Councils never need to justify spending
questions.explain_es: 'Councils must justify every decision.'

questions.q: Ms Njeri says a library is one of the few places where you are welcome without buying anything.
questions.explain_es: 'A library is one of the few places where you don't have to buy anything to be welcome.'

questions.q: Mr Hollis says that borrowing from libraries has been rising steadily.
questions.explain_es: Dice: 'Borrowing has fallen steadily'.

dictation: A library is one of the few places where you don't have to buy anything to be welcome.
That's data a finance committee can use.

title: Metals from the Abyss
focus: Cause and effect language (stem from, give rise to, result in, bring about)

lines.text: Good afternoon. Today's topic is mining the deep sea, an idea that has moved from science fiction to serious commercial planning.
On parts of the ocean floor, thousands of metres down, lie lumps of rock the size of potatoes, known as nodules. They contain metals such as nickel, cobalt and manganese, which are used in batteries.
The demand for these metals stems largely from the transition to electric vehicles, and that demand has given rise to a lot of interest in the seabed.
Supporters argue that mining nodules could result in less environmental damage than digging up land, where forests are cleared and communities displaced.
That's a serious argument, and I don't want to dismiss it. Mining on land has caused significant harm, and the harm is well documented.

But the deep sea is different from a quarry. It's a slow environment, where life grows slowly and recovers even more slowly. Disturbance there may bring about changes that last for decades, perhaps much longer.
Moreover, mining machines would stir up clouds of sediment, which could drift far from the site and smother animals that filter their food from the water.
The nodules themselves are habitat, too. Remove them, and you remove the surfaces on which some animals live.
What worries many scientists is that we don't yet know enough to predict the consequences. Our knowledge of these ecosystems is thin, and a great many species haven't been described.
Who decides? Seabed in international waters is governed by an international body, which is responsible for granting licences and writing rules.
It has been criticised from both sides, by companies who say it's too slow, and by campaigners who say it's too close to the industry.
Meanwhile, recycling and new battery designs that need fewer of these metals could reduce demand, which might make the whole debate less urgent.
So I'd say this: the decision shouldn't be driven by commercial pressure but by evidence, and the evidence isn't in yet.
For next week, please read the two position papers and be ready to argue for one side, whichever you personally prefer.

questions.q: How does the lecturer treat the argument that seabed mining may harm less than land mining?
options: She takes it seriously but is not persuaded
questions.explain_es: Actitud. 'That's a serious argument, and I don't want to dismiss it.' Pero luego describe los riesgos del fondo marino.

questions.q: What does she imply by 'the evidence isn't in yet'?
options: Scientists refuse to study the sea
Decisions should wait for more knowledge
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. La decisión debe basarse en pruebas que aún no existen.

questions.q: Why does she mention that nodules are habitat?
options: To explain where the metals come from
To show that removing them itself causes harm
questions.explain_es: Propósito. 'Remove them, and you remove the surfaces on which some animals live.'

questions.q: How does she describe the international body that governs the seabed?
options: Criticised by both industry and campaigners
questions.explain_es: 'Criticised from both sides, by companies who say it's too slow, and by campaigners who say it's too close to the industry.'

questions.q: She says the deep sea recovers quickly from disturbance.
questions.explain_es: Dice: 'life grows slowly and recovers even more slowly'.

questions.q: She says demand for the metals stems largely from the shift to electric vehicles.
questions.explain_es: 'The demand for these metals stems largely from the transition to electric vehicles.'

dictation: Mining on land has caused significant harm, and the harm is well documented.
Our knowledge of these ecosystems is thin, and a great many species haven't been described.

title: Why Teachers Leave
focus: Emphatic adverbials (not least, if anything, above all, to some extent)

lines.text: Mr Anand, your school has been advertising a maths post for a year. Why is it so hard to find teachers?
There are several reasons, not least the pay, which hasn't kept pace with what graduates can earn elsewhere. If anything, the gap has widened.
Is it just money?
No. Above all, it's workload. Teachers I speak to say it's the marking, the paperwork and the constant inspection that wear them down, rather than the teaching itself.
And yet people still enter the profession.
They do, and many of them are exceptional. But to some extent we lose them within five years, which is a waste of the training.
What would persuade them to stay?
Time, mostly. What's more, trust. Teachers want to be treated as professionals who can be relied on to make decisions, not as people to be monitored.
Some would say that accountability matters.
It does, and I'm not against it. But it has to be proportionate. Taken too far, it produces anxiety rather than quality.
Are there any positive signs?
A few. Some schools have cut the amount of written feedback required, and the early results, if anything, show that pupils haven't suffered.
That's interesting.
It is, though I'd urge caution. It's early days, and we shouldn't draw firm conclusions from a handful of cases.
What would you say to someone considering teaching?
That it's still the best job I know, bar none, for the right person. But go in with your eyes open, and find a school that looks after its staff.
Thank you.

questions.q: How does Mr Anand feel about accountability in schools?
options: He opposes any form of accountability
He thinks it is entirely useless
He supports it if it is proportionate
He wants it to be increased
questions.explain_es: Actitud. 'It does, and I'm not against it. But it has to be proportionate.'

questions.q: What does he imply by 'we shouldn't draw firm conclusions from a handful of cases'?
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Los primeros resultados son prometedores pero 'it's early days'.

questions.q: Why does he advise newcomers to find a school that looks after its staff?
options: To help them make the job sustainable
questions.explain_es: Propósito. Es un consejo para entrar 'with your eyes open' en una profesión exigente.

questions.q: What does he say about teachers who leave within five years?
questions.explain_es: 'We lose them within five years, which is a waste of the training.'

questions.q: Mr Anand says that teachers value being trusted as professionals.
questions.explain_es: 'Teachers want to be treated as professionals who can be relied on to make decisions.'

questions.q: He says the pay gap between teaching and other graduate jobs has narrowed.
questions.explain_es: Dice: 'If anything, the gap has widened.'

dictation: Taken too far, it produces anxiety rather than quality.
Teachers want to be treated as professionals who can be relied on to make decisions, not as people to be monitored.

title: With the Benefit of Hindsight
focus: Language of hindsight (with hindsight, in retrospect, looking back, should have)

lines.text: Several years on, what should we have learned from the pandemic? Doctor Rossi?
That preparation is cheap compared with improvisation. Looking back, many countries had plans, but they were plans nobody had rehearsed.
With hindsight, I'd add that communication was the weakest point. Messages changed so often that the public couldn't tell what was settled and what was provisional.
That's difficult, though. Scientists were learning in real time. In retrospect, it might have helped to say openly, we don't know yet.
Quite. The temptation is to sound certain, and the result, when advice changes, is that trust takes a hit.
Is it fair to judge decisions made under that pressure?
It's fair to learn from them, but we should avoid the benefit of hindsight when assigning blame. Nobody could have known then what we know now.
I'd draw a distinction, though. Some errors were foreseeable. Hospitals had been warned about shortages of protective equipment well before any outbreak.
Granted. Those were failures of attention rather than of knowledge.
What about the longer-term effects, such as education?
That's where I think we paid the highest price. Children lost months of schooling, and the impact fell hardest on those who were already disadvantaged.
It's a case where, looking back, the closure of schools may have been prolonged longer than the evidence justified in some places, although it was a hard call at the time.
Is there any reason to be hopeful?
Cooperation between researchers produced vaccines in record time. That shows what can be done when barriers come down.
I'd only add that the barriers came back as soon as the urgency faded. The real test is whether we keep the lessons.
A fitting note to end on. Thank you both.

questions.q: What does Professor Mbeki identify as the weakest point?
questions.explain_es: Actitud. 'Communication was the weakest point.'

questions.q: What does Professor Mbeki imply by 'the barriers came back as soon as the urgency faded'?
options: Cooperation tends to decline without a crisis
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Pregunta si se mantendrán las lecciones: 'The real test is whether we keep the lessons.'

questions.q: Why does Doctor Rossi mention warnings about protective equipment?
options: To argue that some errors were foreseeable
To prove that nobody could have known
questions.explain_es: Propósito. 'Some errors were foreseeable.'

questions.q: According to Doctor Rossi, who bore the heaviest cost of school closures?
questions.explain_es: 'The impact fell hardest on those who were already disadvantaged.'

questions.q: Professor Mbeki says nobody should ever learn from decisions made under pressure.
questions.explain_es: Dice: 'It's fair to learn from them'.

questions.q: Doctor Rossi says that admitting 'we don't know yet' might have helped.
questions.explain_es: 'In retrospect, it might have helped to say openly, we don't know yet.'

dictation: Nobody could have known then what we know now.
The real test is whether we keep the lessons.

title: The Gap Between What Should Happen and What Does

lines.text: Jonah, you write for television comedy. Where do jokes come from?
Mostly from frustration, which is to say, from an observation that something doesn't quite make sense. The joke is the gap between what should happen and what does.
That sounds more like an analysis than a punchline.
Ha. It's rather like explaining a joke, which, as everyone knows, is a bit like dissecting a frog: you learn a lot, but the frog dies.
Fair. Is there a rule for writing a good one?
Be specific. A vague joke is a dead joke. Not a dog, but a small, anxious terrier in a tiny raincoat.
What about the British habit of understatement? You can say it's a bit chilly when it's snowing.
It's wonderful, because the speaker is pretending nothing is wrong while the audience knows everything is. The comedy lives in the distance between the two.
And does it travel? American audiences?
Some of it. Irony is trickier. If you say that was brilliant after something terrible, one audience laughs, another assumes you mean it.
So how do you check?
We test scripts on a room of people. Rarely do we guess correctly which line will land, which is humbling.
Is there anything you won't joke about?
Not so much a list of topics as a question of who the target is. Joking at the expense of someone with power is one thing; at the expense of someone who has none is quite another.
A principle rather than a rule.
Exactly. And I'd say the best comedy is generous. It lets you laugh at yourself first.
Good advice for all of us. Thank you.

questions.q: What is Jonah's attitude to explaining jokes?
options: Serious, believing that it improves them
Angry, believing that it is rude
Wry, acknowledging that it spoils them
Bored, believing that it is pointless
questions.explain_es: Actitud. 'Explaining a joke is a bit like dissecting a frog: you learn a lot, but the frog dies.'

questions.q: What does Jonah imply by 'Rarely do we guess correctly which line will land'?
questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Dice que es 'humbling', es decir, que los guionistas se equivocan a menudo.

questions.q: Why does Jonah describe a terrier in a raincoat?
options: To illustrate the value of specific detail
questions.explain_es: Propósito. 'Be specific. A vague joke is a dead joke.'

questions.q: How does Jonah decide what to joke about?
options: By testing on a single person
By checking a list of banned topics
By considering who the target is
questions.explain_es: 'Not so much a list of topics as a question of who the target is.'

questions.q: Jonah says the best comedy is generous and lets you laugh at yourself first.
questions.explain_es: 'The best comedy is generous. It lets you laugh at yourself first.'

questions.q: He says irony works equally well with every audience.
questions.explain_es: Dice: 'Irony is trickier... another assumes you mean it.'

dictation: A vague joke is a dead joke.
The comedy lives in the distance between the two.

title: Inside the Seed Bank
focus: Relative clauses (whose, of which, where) in descriptions

lines.text: Welcome to the Highland Seed Bank. Before we go in, a quick word about what we do, since it's not what most visitors expect.
I imagined rows of plants, to be honest.
Most people do. In fact, the collection, most of which is stored as dry seed, takes up far less space than a garden would.
How do you keep seeds alive for so long?
By drying them thoroughly and then freezing them. Seeds whose moisture is low enough can survive for decades, even centuries in some species, though it varies widely.
Do they ever go off?
Eventually. That's why we test samples regularly. If the proportion that germinate falls below a set level, we grow the plants again and collect fresh seed.
That sounds like a lot of work.
It is. It's a kind of insurance, a record of crop varieties, many of which have vanished from farms, kept in case they're needed.
Needed for what?
For breeding, mostly. A variety whose flavour is ordinary might carry a gene that resists a disease, and that's the sort of thing a plant breeder is hunting for.
And is it just crops?
No. We also keep wild relatives of crops, as well as wildflowers from the region, some of which are down to a handful of sites.
Is the collection safe?
Reasonably. It's built in a place where flooding is unlikely, and half the samples are duplicated in another country, in case something happens here.
Does anyone use it?
All the time. Farmers can request seed of old varieties, and we've had cases where a lost local variety was returned to the community that originally grew it.
That's moving.
It is. Shall we go in? Mind the cold, it's kept well below freezing.

options: Proud of its role as insurance
questions.explain_es: Actitud. 'It's a kind of insurance... kept in case they're needed.'

questions.q: What does the guide imply by 'it's not what most visitors expect'?

questions.explain_es: Implicatura. Sam confirma: 'I imagined rows of plants.'

questions.q: Why does she mention a variety with ordinary flavour?
options: To show that unremarkable plants may carry useful genes
To compare the taste of crops
questions.explain_es: Propósito. 'A variety whose flavour is ordinary might carry a gene that resists a disease.'

questions.q: What happens if the proportion of seeds that germinate falls too low?
options: Plants are regrown and fresh seed is collected
The sample is sold to farmers
questions.explain_es: 'We grow the plants again and collect fresh seed.'

questions.q: The guide says seeds can survive for decades only if kept at room temperature.
questions.explain_es: Dice que se secan y luego se congelan: 'By drying them thoroughly and then freezing them.'

questions.explain_es: 'Half the samples are duplicated in another country.'

dictation: It's a kind of insurance, a record of crop varieties, many of which have vanished from farms, kept in case they're needed.

title: Clearing the Air
focus: Paraphrasing and reflecting back (what I'm hearing is…, you're saying that…)

lines.text: Thank you both for agreeing to this. My role isn't to decide who's right, but to help you find a way of working together. Dev, would you like to begin?
Sure. Since Karen took over the project, my ideas have been dismissed in meetings. She says things like, that's not realistic, without explaining why.
So what I'm hearing is that you feel your contributions aren't being given a fair hearing. Is that right?
Exactly.
Karen, how does that sound to you?
Honestly, it surprises me. I've never meant to dismiss anyone. I've been under a lot of pressure to hit the deadline, and I suppose I've been brisk.
You're saying that the tone came from the deadline, not from a view of Dev's ideas?
Yes. I think his ideas are good. I just haven't had time to discuss them properly.
That's news to me. I assumed you didn't rate me.
Dev, how does it feel to hear that?
Better, honestly. If she'd said that in the meeting, I'd have saved myself weeks of resentment.
Karen, what do you take from that?
That I should explain my reasons, even briefly. A short sentence would have saved a lot of trouble.
Could we agree on something practical? For example, a short weekly slot to go through Dev's proposals?
That would work, provided it's protected time and not squeezed in at the end of the day.
Agreed. I'll put it in the diary, and I'll try to say why when I turn something down.
Then let me summarise. Karen will explain her reasons, and you'll have a weekly slot. We'll meet again in a month to see whether it's working.
Thanks. It's a relief to have talked.

questions.explain_es: Actitud. 'My ideas have been dismissed in meetings.'

questions.q: What does Dev imply by 'I'd have saved myself weeks of resentment'?

He wants Karen to be replaced

questions.explain_es: 'Provided it's protected time and not squeezed in at the end of the day.'

title: Reading in a Distracted Age
focus: Verb + preposition patterns (object to, insist on, result from, account for, put up with)

lines.text: Welcome to our session on reading in the digital age. Mr Abara, many people complain that nobody reads novels any more. Do you agree?
I object to the way that's put. People still read, but they're coping with more distractions. I'd insist on that distinction, because the first claim is gloomy and the second is useful.
I'd go along with that. The statistics are mixed, and much of the gloom results from comparing today with a golden age that may never have existed.
Ms Lindholm, you review for a newspaper. Has your work changed?
Considerably. Readers now react within minutes, so I'm no longer just writing for an audience, but conversing with it. I wouldn't dispense with that for anything, although it can be exhausting.
I'd add that the pressure to publish quickly hasn't improved the quality of criticism. There's a case for reviews that take their time.
I can't disagree. Haste accounts for many shallow reviews, and I include some of my own.
What about long novels? Do readers still have the patience?
Some do. Longer books have proved more popular than anyone predicted, which suggests that readers are prepared to put up with demanding work if it rewards them.
If you ask me, readers look forward to being absorbed. It's become a rarer pleasure, which perhaps makes it more valuable.
Mr Abara, do you worry about competing with video and games?
Not especially. A novel offers something they can't: it relies on the reader's imagination, so the experience is more intimate. I'd rather cater for that than imitate a film.
Any advice for people who want to read more?
Set aside a regular time and stick to it. It's about habit, not willpower.
And don't feel guilty about abandoning a book. Life's too short to persevere with something you dislike.
A good note to end on. Thank you.
